$comment: THE SWIM IS A MORNING SESSION AND THE RUN IS AN EVENING ONE, swapped 2026-09-03 on his ruling.
Until then the morning slot held the run or the bike on all four lifting days and the swim sat
after the lift at about 9 pm. That contradicted the swim plan, which measures its 1,000 m goal
against the morning slot, and it contradicted itself: morning cardio was scheduled on days that
structurally follow a 9 pm swim.
It was put to him as three shapes with the cost of each, not as a fix. The swap won because it
preserves every count and the rest rule while moving two things; the alternatives either starved
the run programme or dropped the swim below the 3 to 4 a week its own plan states. The costs he
took on are written in week.assignedDays.why and are about habit rather than arithmetic.
Run, bike and swim. Separate from program.json because it is not organised by gym day and does
not have a set/rep/rest shape. Evidence for every number is in
HealthOS/knowledge/training-programme-evidence.md.
THE SCHEDULING RULE THAT MAKES THIS FIT, and the reason nothing he already does had to be
traded away: Robineau 2016 found strength gains were LOWER when the aerobic piece followed the
lift immediately (0 h) than at 6 h or 24 h. So the running goes in a morning slot he is not
currently using, against a 9 pm swim that is 12+ hours away.
His lift-then-swim stack on the same evening is inside that 6 h window and STAYS ANYWAY. He has
done it for months and the back squat went 135 to 180 lb across that period. His own log
outranks a guideline derived from rugby players doing a different pairing.
REBUILT FROM HIS OWN RECORD ON 2026-10-04, on his ruling of that evening: "the running, I think
the plan makes no sense for what I can actually do, it was built on me never having run before,
same for bike." And: "rebuild everything based on what I can do ... the workouts time-wise is
mostly programming, whatever you put there I'll do, but I want it to be grounded."
Both plans used to assume a beginner: the run was the Bertelsen 2018 novice 3 km arm on a
treadmill, the bike a 4x4 with "the first two sessions deliberately undercooked". His record says
otherwise: four outdoor runs since 2026-08-24 of 4.5 to 5.0 km on the watch, a continuous 5.03 km
on 2026-10-03, 29 runs in 2023; and on the bike two 31 to 35 minute rides in 2026 plus five
43 to 48 minute outdoor rides in 2024. Every number in run and bike now carries its grounding in a
`$why` beside it (his log, or a source fetched on 2026-10-04 and quoted verbatim), or is labelled a
judgment. The old plans are in git at ed7b28a.
TWO RULES FROM HIM THAT SHAPE WHAT RENDERS (email 2026-10-04 19:35). (1) Every distance a page
shows is the number his watch shows: TOTAL session distance, walks included, never a running-only
figure we computed. Running-only figures live in `$` fields and say so. (2) Session length is ours
to set: every run and bike session states its total minutes.
TECHNIQUE CUES, added 2026-08-16. Each discipline carries a `cues` array; every cue is a TEST he can
perform with a binary result. `confidence` is one of evidence / convention / contested, and
"convention" means coaching practice with no study behind it, said plainly. The run cues were
rewritten for outdoor running on 2026-10-04: the treadmill cues (belt speed, incline, safety clip,
console checks) went with the treadmill.
SWIM LEFT THIS FILE on 2026-08-26. It is content/swim/plan.json now, rendered by /swim, and the
paragraphs recording the three false claims corrected on 2026-08-21 went with it. This file is
run and bike, plus the week that holds all three.

slots.$comment: Where each thing lives in a week. Pool times are his, given 2026-08-15.

morning.name: Morning
morning.what: Nothing scheduled. The pool is open at 6:00 if an evening swim gets missed.
morning.why: The morning slot has been tried twice, in August and on 2026-09-03, and did not survive a week either time. His words: "getting up that early will affect my sleep schedule". Everything sits in the evening, where his record says he actually trains.

evening.name: Evening
evening.what: Lift first. Then the swim after every lift, and the walk-run after Session B before it.
evening.why: Lift first, unchanged: the concurrent-training review trends favour lifting before the aerobic piece, and his squat went up while stacking the swim after the gym. The run sits after the shorter session and the swim after the longer one, so no evening carries all three.

run.title: Run
run.startedFrom: A returning runner, not a beginner. Runs of 9 minutes or more on record: 29 in 2023 (including continuous runs of 5.0, 6.0 and 7.5 km), 5 in 2024, 2 in 2025, one treadmill session on 2026-08-18, and since 2026-08-24 four outdoor runs that read 4.54, 5.03, 5.02 and 5.03 km on his watch, 34.7 to 40.1 minutes each, four in 41 days, with a three-week gap. The last, 2026-10-03, was continuous, 34.7 minutes, average running heart rate 155, 31.5 minutes above 140. The one that stayed easy was 2026-08-24: 3 minutes run, 1 minute walk, ten times, 40.1 minutes, 4.54 km, running pace 8:04 per km, running heart rate 125. Source: HealthOS/knowledge/ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md, which an adversary re-ran the same day.
run.$startedFromRunningOnly: RUNNING-ONLY FIGURES, never rendered (his rule, 2026-10-04: a page shows the watch total). Running seconds = step rate 140 or more. Kilometres of running in those four sessions: 3.62, 4.19, 4.37, 4.94. Running pace 8:04, 7:13, 7:00, 6:50 per km. Walking pace on 2026-08-24: 0.92 km in 10.9 minutes, about 11:50 per km.
why: Start from what he has done, at the effort he has shown he can hold easily, and let the clock grow
10% a week. Twice a week rather than once, because his record is one run a week with gaps, and
the same weekly load split into two shorter runs is the gentler way to carry it on the legs of a
heavy runner (his weight is in HealthOS/CURRENT.md and is not copied here). That last clause is a judgment, not a finding.

howHard.primary: The talk test. You must be able to say a full sentence out loud without gasping. If you cannot, walk until you can, then run on slower.
howHard.secondary: If you want a number, keep your heart rate under 140. On your one easy run that meant about 8:00 per km.
howHard.$why: THE TALK TEST is the intensity instruction of the injury trial this plan's load rules come from. Bertelsen 2018, fetched 2026-10-04 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/, verbatim: "All participants were instructed to have at least one day with no running between each session and to run with a moderate intensity i.e. being able to converse without breathlessness." THE 140 HAS NO STUDY BEHIND IT; it is the plan's old ceiling, kept as a convention. What his own record adds (ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md, E9 and recommendations): only 2026-08-24, at 8:04 per km running pace with one-minute walks, stayed mostly under 140 (2.4 of 40.1 minutes above). At 7:13 per km on 2026-08-30 he was above 140 for 18.5 of 39.3 minutes. The watch put his aerobic threshold at 134 to 136 on each run, so 140 sits just above it. So "about 8:00 per km" is his number, not a population one.

pace.check: Look at the pace once in each run block. Faster than 8:00 per km means slow down.
pace.$why: GROUNDED IN HIS LOG, not a source. 480 s/km is 8:00, rounded from his 8:04 running pace on 2026-08-24, the one run that stayed under 140. 720 s/km is 12:00, rounded from that session's walking (0.92 km in 10.9 min, about 11:50). The page uses these two numbers to compute the "about X km on the watch" line for each week, total distance including walks, which is the figure his watch shows. Checked against the session they come from: 2026-08-24 as written (29.2 min running, 10.9 min walking) computes to 3.65 + 0.91 = 4.56 km against 4.54 on the watch. THE CHECK IS 8:00 because 8:04 is the only pace on his record that stayed under 140 (one run, n = 1); at 7:13 he was above 140 for 18.5 of 39.3 minutes. A faster threshold would permit a pace his data has never shown to be easy. The pace stays fixed for all eight weeks so distance and speed never rise together.

weeks.note: Reassess here before deciding whether to keep climbing or hold.

$weeksWhy: WEEK 1 SITS BETWEEN HIS AVERAGE WEEK AND HIS BIGGEST, AT EASY EFFORT, SPLIT IN TWO. Running-only
figures, never rendered: his four outdoor runs since 2026-08-24 hold 17.1 km of running over about
six weeks, about 3.0 km a week on average and about 2.3 km a week over the last four (a three-week
gap); his two most recent single weeks held 4.4 and 4.9. Week 1 is 2 sessions of 15 running minutes,
30 minutes a week, which at 8:00 per km is about 3.75 km of running: above his average, below his two
recent weeks, and level with the old plan's top week (3.8). On the watch that is about 2.5 km a
session, walks included, against his 4.5 to 5.0 km single runs. JUDGMENT: no study sets the start
for a returning runner. ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md's corrected inference reads "The plan's own rules
point to dropping back toward its weekly sizes, not holding where he is", and week 1 follows it.
Nothing in his record shows he tolerated his recent weeks well or badly: there is no injury data,
and 2026-10-03 was hard by the watch (6.0 minutes at or above its anaerobic threshold).
WHY HE IS OUTSIDE THE NOVICE TRIAL NOW, and why its rules still apply. Bertelsen 2018 (fetched
2026-10-04, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/) admitted "Individuals with BMI 30-35,
age 18-65 years, no previous running experience (less than 10km combined the last year)". He has
about 20 km since 2026-08-18, so the trial no longer describes him. Its authors write that "other
sub-groups may possibly tolerate a start-to-run distance of more than 6km per week while remaining
at low risk of running-related injury (E.g. obese individuals with previous sports experience).
Further studies are needed" (quoted across a sentence break). No evidence fixes his start. Its load
rule is still the nearest guide: "In both programs, the weekly running distance was increased by 10%
each week throughout the follow-up." Injuries: "Two participants were injured in the 3km
intervention (6.9%). Five participants were injured in the 6km intervention (18.5%)."
THE PROGRESSION. Three run blocks a session, one minute walking after each, 5 minutes walking first.
Each block grows 30 seconds a week: 15, 16.5, 18, 19.5, 21, 22.5, 24, 25.5 running minutes a session,
increases of 10.0, 9.1, 8.3, 7.7, 7.1, 6.7 and 6.3%, none above the trial's 10%. Week 8 is 51 running
minutes a week, about 6.4 km of running: above the trial's 6 km STARTING dose, reached by its own 10%
rule. The trial ran four weeks; weeks 5 to 8 extrapolate that rule past what it measured, which is why
week 8 says reassess. The walks: the trial split its running "into shorter intervals with walking at
an easy/comfortable pace in the pauses between each interval", and on his record the one-minute walks
are what kept 2026-08-24 under 140. Blocks of 5:00 and up are inside what he has run without stopping
WHY THREE BLOCKS AND THE 5:00 WALK FIRST: judgment. Three keeps the watch screen simple; the 5:00 walk
is the warm-up and matches the old plan's opening walk.
rules: Never add more than 10% in a week, and never add distance and speed in the same week.
Pace stays near 8:00 per km for all eight weeks. Only the run minutes grow.
The run ends when the last block ends, however good you feel.
A missed week means repeat the last week you completed, not jump to where the calendar says.
Any pain that changes how you walk means stop and say so. Shin and knee are the two to watch.
run.$rulesWhy: Rules 1 and 4 are the old plan's and stay: rule 1 is Bertelsen's ~10% a week (quoted in $weeksWhy), and rule 4 is the reading of that rule after a gap. Rule 2 is how rule 1 is kept: if speed is fixed, only time can rise. Rule 3 is from his record, not a paper: by calendar week, every one of his four outdoor runs broke a plan rule and held 2 to 5 times the prescribed running (ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md, finding 10). Rule 5 is unchanged.

cues.name: Step rate
cues.cue: Keep the short, quick step you already have. Your recent runs sit at 154 to 161 steps a minute. Step rate is how many times a foot lands in one minute, both feet counted. To measure it, two minutes into the first run block, count every time your RIGHT foot lands for 30 seconds.
cues.test: PASS = 38 or more right-foot landings in 30 seconds, which is 152 steps a minute. FAIL = 37 or fewer: take shorter, quicker steps at the same pace and count again in the next block. Do not speed up to fix it.
cues.why: Raising step rate is the one form change with a consistent measured effect on how hard your legs get hit, and you already made it: at the same speed your runs this year sit above every run you did in 2023. The job now is to keep it at the slower easy pace, where a long, loping step is the easy mistake.
cues.grounding: HIS DATA (ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md, finding 5, adversary-checked): within each speed band every 2026 run sits at 154 to 161 steps a minute and every 2023 run at 148 to 154 (n = 4 against n = 16), no overlap; run-to-run noise +-2.3. 152 is 154 minus that noise, rounded to a count a hand can make (38 x 4). Note the session average on the Now tab includes the walks (141.8 on 2026-08-24), so it cannot be used for this check. THE EVIDENCE for step rate itself: Figueiredo I, Reis e Silva M, Sousa JE. Cureus. 2025;17(8):e90322, fetched 2026-10-04 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12440572/, verbatim: "A moderate increase in cadence (typically 5-10%) led to consistent biomechanical improvements, including reduced vertical ground reaction forces, lower loading rates, shorter stride length, and improved lower limb alignment" and "cadence modification did not negatively affect metabolic cost". Caveats kept from the earlier pass: Cureus is a low-barrier journal, the review covers normal-weight runners only, and no step-rate study at BMI 30 to 35 was found.

cues.name: One change only
cues.cue: Step rate is the only thing about your running form you look after on this plan. Whatever part of your foot hits the ground first, leave it alone. That is called your footstrike: heel first is a rearfoot strike, ball of the foot first is a forefoot strike. If an app, a video or a friend tells you your footstrike is wrong, the answer is no. You also do not work on posture, arm swing, leaning forward or breathing rhythm. Pain that changes the way you walk means stop the run, not change your form.
cues.test: Before you start the watch, name to yourself the one form thing you are working on today. PASS = it is step rate and nothing else. FAIL = it is anything else, in which case drop it and run with step rate only.
cues.why: Switching a heel striker onto the forefoot moves load off the knee and onto the calf and Achilles tendon, the tissue least prepared to take it at your weight, and it makes running harder at the same speed. There is no prospective evidence that the switch prevents injury. And if you change two things at once and something starts hurting, you cannot tell which one did it.
cues.grounding: Anderson LM, Bonanno DR, Hart HF, Barton CJ. Sports Med. 2020;50(5):885-917, abstract fetched 2026-10-04 at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=31823338&rettype=abstract&retmode=text, verbatim: "combined with the associated shift in loading profile (i.e., greater ankle and plantarflexor loading) found in this review, changing strike pattern cannot be recommended for an uninjured RFS runner." The one-change-at-a-time packaging is coaching convention, hence the label.

cues.name: The passage
cues.cue: Pick about 30 words you know by heart and use the SAME words every run. Say them out loud at normal speaking volume to gauge how hard you are working. You have two gauges, the passage and the watch, and whichever one is stricter wins. If the passage fails, you slow down even if the watch reads under 140. If the watch reads over 140, you slow down even if the words came out fine.
cues.test: Say the passage out loud halfway through each run block. PASS = all the words with at most one break to breathe, AND the watch reads 140 or below. If you are unsure whether you broke to breathe, count it as a break. FAIL = walk for one minute, then run the rest of the block slower. The clock keeps running and the session ends at the same time.
cues.why: Two gauges will disagree, and letting the stricter one win means a wrong wrist reading can only make you go easier, never harder. Fixed words matter because an improvised sentence gets shorter as you tire, so the test gets easier exactly when it needs to hold. On your 2026-10-03 run the watch read over 140 for 31.5 of 34.7 minutes; this is the cue that stops that becoming the easy run.
cues.grounding: Bertelsen 2018 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/, fetched 2026-10-04) used a talk instruction only: "run with a moderate intensity i.e. being able to converse without breathlessness". Vieira AM et al. Rev Cardiovasc Med. 2022;23(7):225, fetched 2026-10-04 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11266803/, verbatim: "Workload, oxygen uptake, and heart rate in the last positive stage of the TT were not different from the same parameters related to the first ventilatory threshold." CONTESTED because that review is of cardiac patients, and its authors write "Evidence is missing regarding the applicability of the talk test in a more heterogeneous population". The 140 is a convention (see howHard.$why). The walk-a-minute fix replaces the old belt drop: there is no belt outdoors; judgment.

cues.name: Hills
cues.cue: On a climb, keep the effort and let the pace drop. Slow down or walk up it until the talk test passes again. A flat loop makes every other check on this page easier to read.
cues.test: At the top of any climb, say your passage. PASS = all the words with at most one break. FAIL = walk until it passes, then run on at the slower pace.
cues.why: Your one hilly run, 2026-09-26, climbed 111 m against 29 to 35 m on the others. A climb at the same pace is more work, so judge it by the talk test, not the watch pace.
cues.grounding: HIS DATA, ANALYSIS-2026-10-04-RUN.md finding 2: at matched speed (6:57 to 7:35 per km) heart rate was 130 on 2026-08-24, 148 on 08-30, 146 on 09-26 and 159 on 10-03, and the analysis names the 111 m climb on 09-26 as one of four confounds it CANNOT separate (walk breaks, time of day, same-day lifting and swimming, route). So the cue does not claim the hill caused the 146; it asks him to judge the climb by effort, which needs no such claim. No study cited. CONVENTION.

cues.name: Walks and stopping
cues.cue: The walks are part of the run: keep walking through them and do not stand still. Stopping for any other reason is different and always correct: pain that changes the way you walk, dizziness, chest pain, or anything that feels wrong means you stop and walk home.
cues.test: Three checks. (1) Before the first walk, start the watch on an outdoor run. PASS = it shows a heart rate before you set off. (2) In every walk you keep moving. PASS = no standing rests. (3) A stop for pain, dizziness or anything wrong is a PASS, every time.
cues.why: The injury trial behind the load rules walked its pauses; it never stood. Starting the watch before the first walk keeps the whole session as one record, which is what the Now tab and the watch distance on the Plan tab compare against.
cues.grounding: Bertelsen 2018, fetched 2026-10-04 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6253747/, verbatim: "The running distance in both programs was split up into shorter intervals with walking at an easy/comfortable pace in the pauses between each interval." CONVENTION because the trial never compared walking against standing.

cues.name: Shoes
cues.cue: Choose running shoes on fit first, using the test below. If two pairs both pass the fit test, take the softer and more cushioned one. Do not pay extra for anything sold as stability or motion control, and do not trust a shoe because the box says it is for heavier runners.
cues.test: Do this late in the day, in the socks you will run in. Pull the insole out of the shoe first. The insole is the loose flat liner you can lift out from inside. Put it on the floor and stand on it. Three checks, all three must pass. (1) Look down at the gap in front of your longest toe, which is not always the big toe. PASS = the insole extends at least a thumb width past the end of it. (2) Look at the sides of the insole. PASS = no part of your foot hangs over the edge anywhere. (3) Put the insole back, lace the shoe and walk 20 steps. The heel cup is the stiff cup at the back of the shoe that wraps around your heel. PASS = your heel stays down inside it and does not lift away as you step. Any one fail means it is the wrong shoe, whatever the price, the brand or the review says.
cues.why: The trial split its runners at the middle of their own body mass, 78.2 kg for men, so at your weight you sit above even its heavier half. In that half the harder shoe still pointed the wrong way, but the range around it ran from 25 percent lower risk to roughly double, so it could be chance. The question is unsettled for a man your size, not settled against cushioning. Fit is where runners actually get hurt in month one: a shoe too short or too narrow gives black toenails and forefoot pain inside a few weeks.
cues.grounding: Malisoux L, Delattre N, Urhausen A, Theisen D. Am J Sports Med. 2020;48(2):473-480, abstract fetched 2026-10-04 at https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=31877062&rettype=abstract&retmode=text, verbatim: "lighter runners had a higher injury risk in hard shoes (SHR, 1.80 [95% CI, 1.09-2.98]) while heavier runners did not (SHR, 1.23 [95% CI, 0.75-2.03])" and "the relative protective effect of greater shoe cushioning was found only in lighter runners." CONTESTED for him: the heavier subgroup is underpowered, not null. The three fit checks are CONVENTION.

run.cuesNote:
WHAT WAS DROPPED, one line each.

1. ALL FOUR TREADMILL CUES (belt speed, incline zero, the safety clip, the console unit test), with the treadmill. He runs outdoors.
2. "RAISE YOUR STEP RATE 5 PERCENT." He already did: his 2026 runs sit above every 2023 run at the same speed. The cue now holds the step he has.
3. THE "RUN QUIETLY" CUE, the footstrike video and the 180 steps a minute target, as before: the sound does not track the force, and 180 is not his number.

MYTHS STILL WORTH NAMING: 180 steps a minute is not universal (Leacox 2025); heel striking is not wrong for an uninjured runner (Anderson 2020); heavy runners do not provably need maximum cushioning, nor provably not (Malisoux 2020).
run.$scheduleNote: TWO A WEEK, Tuesday and Friday after Session B, as week.assignedDays sets it (his ruling 2026-09-04). Two things the record says that this file does not settle. (1) He has not run on those days: his four outdoor runs were a Monday, a Sunday and two Saturdays. (2) Robineau 2016 (abstract fetched 2026-10-04, https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=25546450&rettype=abstract&retmode=text): "Gains in maximal strength for bench press and half squat were lower in C-0h compared with that in C-6h, C-24h, and STR." A run straight after Session B is the 0 h case. Both are his call, not this file's; the first is the open question in the 2026-10-04 report.

bike.title: Bike
bike.startedFrom: HIS RIDING, read from the 2026-10-04 Samsung export (exercise_type 15003 = stationary bike, 11007 = outdoor cycling, per HealthOS/server/import-watch-sessions.mjs; local times from each row's time_offset). Stationary bike: 42 sessions. In 2023 and 2024, 39 of them, almost all 5 to 15 minutes (longest 20.1), average heart rate 89 to 125: warm-ups. In 2026, two real rides: 2026-08-19 06:10, 35.1 minutes, average 120, max 143; and 2026-09-26 14:10, 31.6 minutes, average 137, max 155, starting 33 minutes after his run of that day ended. Outdoor: five rides he started himself between 2024-04-21 and 2024-08-12, 42.7 to 47.6 minutes, 8.9 to 10.4 km, 12 to 14 km/h average, average heart rate 127 to 139, max 163 to 174; two longer rows with no source_type and no heart rate, from a different device id (13.3 km in 66 minutes, 19.0 km in 103 minutes; which device is unverified). Of the 43 outdoor rows, 9 he started himself (source_type 1: the five above, two on 2022-12-23, one on 2023-01-31, one 2.57 km on 2024-09-12), 32 are the watch's own detection (source_type 4, fragments of 3 to 52 minutes) and 2 are the blank rows. Nothing outdoors he started since 2024-09-12. No ride on record shows a 4 by 4 shape, so no interval session is assumed. Type 15006 (11 sessions, 2022 to 2025) is not mapped by the importer and is not counted here.
why: The bike earns its place for one reason. Wilson 2012, abstract fetched 2026-10-04 at
verbatim: "resistance training concurrently with running, but not cycling, resulted in significant
decrements in both hypertrophy and strength." So the bike is where hard aerobic work can go
without costing the legs he lifts with, which is what lets the running stay easy.

protocol.name: Norwegian 4x4, three rounds
protocol.structure: 10 min easy, then 3 rounds of [4 min hard, 3 min easy]
protocol.next: Then 4 rounds: 10 min easy, then 4 rounds of [4 min hard, 3 min easy]. 38 minutes.
protocol.evidenceNote: The 4x4 shape and the 38 minutes are the EX-MET protocol's. The three-round start is a judgment fitted to his rides.
protocol.$why: STARTS AT 31 MINUTES BECAUSE HIS TWO 2026 RIDES WERE 31.6 AND 35.1 MINUTES. Three rounds is the same session length he has already ridden, with hard pieces added. His bike heart rate has touched the hard band but never been held there: 2024 outdoor peaks of 163 to 174, 2026-09-26 peak 155, 2026-08-19 peak 143. Those are peaks, not 4-minute holds, which is one more reason to start at three rounds. The old plan opened at 43 minutes with "the first two sessions deliberately undercooked"; both came from assuming he had never ridden. THE FULL SESSION IS EX-MET'S: Tjonna et al., BMC Public Health 2018, fetched 2026-10-04 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5879994/, verbatim: "The 4-AIT and 1-AIT groups exercise for 38 and 17 min per session, respectively. Both the AIT protocols include a 10-min warm-up and a 3-min cool-down at 60-70% peak heart rate (HRpeak)" (en dashes in the source written as hyphens here), and "a 4-min interval is performed at 85-95% HRpeak (RPE at 15-17 on Borg scale). This is repeated 4 times in the 4-AIT group, separated by 3 min of active recovery at 50-70% HRpeak". 10 + 4x4 + 3x3 + 3 = 38, which is the page's "4 rounds of [4 hard, 3 easy]" after a 10-minute warm-up, the last 3 easy minutes being the cool-down. Three rounds: 10 + 3x4 + 2x3 + 3 = 31. No study sets the step from three to four; the rule for it is a judgment.

howHard.hardPiece: By the end of each 4 minutes you should only be able to get out two or three words at a time. Pick a resistance you could hold for 5 minutes but would not want to.
howHard.heartRate: Aim to finish each hard piece around 150 to 165.
howHard.easyPiece: Genuinely easy. Keep pedalling, get your breath fully back before the next one.
howHard.$why: 150 to 165 is 85 to 95% of 175, the band EX-MET prescribes (quoted in protocol.$why), and HIS RULING of 2026-09-03 keeps it there (see $anchorRuling). His riding has touched it (2024 outdoor peaks 163 to 174, 2026-09-26 peak 155) but never held it for 4 minutes on record.

rules: Three rounds until two rides in a row end every hard piece between 150 and 165. Then four.
bike.$rulesWhy: JUDGMENT, not a source: the step to four rounds waits until the three-round session is landing where EX-MET aims it, measured by the same heart-rate band the cues already check at 2:00. The old rule, "the first two sessions, deliberately undercook the hard pieces", is gone: it assumed he had never ridden.

cues.name: Set the seat, then be able to reproduce it
cues.cue: A gym bike is set by whoever used it last, so the seat height is something you re-set every visit, not something you solve once. Do it before you pedal. Sit on the seat. Put your HEEL on the pedal, not the ball of your foot. Turn the pedals slowly until that pedal is at its lowest point, straight down under you, so the crank (the metal arm the pedal bolts onto) points at the floor. At that point the leg should be straight with the heel still touching, without you leaning to that side to reach. Then slide the foot forward so the pedal sits under the ball of your foot, the pad behind your big toe. That slide is what leaves a small bend in the knee at the bottom of each stroke. Now take a photo of the setting on your phone: the number on the seat post (the vertical tube the seat sits on, which slides up and down inside the frame), or if it has no numbers, the count of holes or notches from the bottom. Next week you set that number first and skip the test. Precision matters less than you think, repeatability matters more: being a centimetre off changes almost nothing, being on a different setting every week means none of your resistance numbers compare.
cues.test: Two looks, both straight down at your own leg, no mirror and no helper. STATIC, before pedalling: heel on the pedal at its lowest point. Is the leg straight without you leaning toward that side? Knee still visibly bent, raise one setting. Cannot reach unless you lean or point your toes down, lower one setting. DYNAMIC, in the first minute of the warm-up with the ball of your foot on the pedal: look down at that knee each time the foot reaches the bottom. Is there a small visible bend in it every single time, never snapping dead straight? Yes, done, leave it. Knee locking straight at the bottom, or toes pointing down to keep contact, lower one setting and look again.
cues.why: The only thing the review calls strong evidence is judging the knee angle while pedalling, which is what the dynamic half of the test does. The heel-on-pedal method itself is workshop convention with no validation behind it, and it is here only because it lands you close, which the same review says is close enough.
cues.grounding: Bini R, Priego-Quesada J. "Methods to determine saddle height in cycling and implications of changes in saddle height in performance and injury risk: A systematic review." Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022;40(4):386-400. DOI 10.1080/02640414.2021.1994727, PMID 34706617. 29,398 records screened, 41 studies included. Verbatim from the abstract I fetched: "Strong evidence suggests that saddle height should be configured using dynamic measurements of the knee angle"; "moderate evidence suggests that changes in saddle height less than 4% of the leg length results in trivial to small changes in lower limb loads, and no effect on oxygen uptake and efficiency"; "there is limited evidence on the effects from changes in saddle height on supramaximal cycling performance or injury risk". Publisher full text 403s, so I read the record via the Europe PMC REST API (URL below). Secondary, also fetched: Bing, Zhang, Wei & Zhang, Front Sports Act Living 2025 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483900/) restates a 25-35 degree knee angle at bottom dead centre and reports static and dynamic knee angles differing by 8.2 +/- 5 degrees. That degree figure is background in that paper, not something it tested, which is why no degree number appears in the cue text.

cues.name: Make the two numbers readable before you start
cues.cue: Every rule below is a glance at two numbers at a named second: your live heart rate, and how long you are into the CURRENT piece. Set both up before the first pedal stroke. On the watch, start a workout that shows heart rate as a number on the screen. The bike console counts total elapsed time for the whole session, so it can never tell you that you are two minutes into interval three. The watch can: press the lap button at the start of every 4 minute effort and again at the start of every 3 minute recovery, so the lap timer always shows time inside the piece you are in. If your watch cannot do laps, set a repeating countdown on your phone, 4 minutes then 3 minutes, and read the countdown instead.
cues.test: Sitting on the bike, before you start: can you see a heart rate number in beats per minute AND a timer you can reset to zero, at the same time, without pressing more than one button? If no, fix it now, before the warm-up.
cues.why: Eight of the checks in this list are unperformable without a live heart rate and interval-relative time, and nothing in the plan establishes either. This is not evidence-based, it is the difference between a rule you can follow and a rule you cannot.

cues.name: Warm up to a heart-rate number, and still finish on time
cues.cue: The 10 easy minutes have a target, not just a duration. Pedal hard enough that your heart rate reads 105 to 123 by minute 8, and hold it to minute 10. For the 3 minute recoveries between efforts, 88 to 123 is fine, and note that is a WIDER band than the warm-up, not the same one. Whatever the number says at minute 8, the warm-up ends at minute 10 and interval 1 starts. Do not extend it. The session is 31 minutes with three rounds and 38 with four, and it stays that long.
cues.test: One look at the watch at minute 8 of the warm-up. Heart rate 105 to 123: hold this resistance and start interval 1 at minute 10. Under 105: add one resistance level, and still start at minute 10. Over 123: drop one level. Then during each 3 minute recovery, one look at 2:00 into it. Above 123: drop one level. Below 88: add one level.
cues.why: The plan currently says "easy", which is a feeling, and the protocol puts percentages on it. The honest gap, corrected 2026-08-28: HRpeak means a peak from a maximal test, and this cue used to say 175 was "the highest number his watch has happened to record". It is not. The export's highest is {PEAK_BPM}, from {PEAK_KIND} on {PEAK_DATE}, and 23 of 60 swims beat 175. So the conclusion the old sentence reached is still right and its reason was wrong: these bands are low, and by a wider margin than was believed. That is still the safe direction for week one. It is not a reason to go looking for the real number, and it is not a reason to prescribe from {PEAK_BPM} either, which is the open question parked on this block.
cues.grounding: Tjonna et al., the EX-MET study protocol, BMC Public Health 2018, a randomised multicentre trial in adults with metabolic syndrome, performed on "cycle or treadmill ergometer (self-selected)". Its 4x4 arm, verbatim: "10-min warm-up" at "60-70% peak heart rate (HRpeak)", "4 x 4 min" at "85-95% HRpeak" with target heart rate "reached within two minutes", "3 min of active recovery at 50-70% HRpeak", "3-min cool-down at 60-70% peak heart rate", 3 times per week, 38 minutes per session. I checked specifically: the protocol paper never defines how HRpeak was measured.

cues.name: Hold the RPM, change the resistance
cues.cue: Cadence means how many complete circles one foot makes in a minute. The console shows it as RPM, sometimes labelled cadence. Pick a number near 80 and keep it there all session, hard minutes and easy ones alike. When the session needs to be harder or easier you change the RESISTANCE LEVEL, never the RPM. One variable, and the RPM is the one you hold still, so that "level 9 for four minutes" means the same thing next Tuesday as it did this Tuesday. If the console shows no RPM at all, count one foot's circles for 15 seconds and multiply by four (20 circles in 15 seconds is 80 RPM), do that once during the warm-up so you know what it feels like at that resistance, and then run the whole session on the resistance rule alone.
cues.test: Look at the RPM readout once per effort, at 2:00, in the same glance as the heart rate, and not before. Below 70: drop one resistance level, and that is the only change you make this interval. Above 95: add one level. Between 70 and 95: leave it alone. That is the entire cadence rule for the session.
cues.why: The real reason is bookkeeping, not physiology: holding cadence makes resistance the only thing that moves, so the numbers you write down mean something a week later. There is a second reason that is arithmetic rather than a study: power equals force times pedal speed, so at the same watts a slower stroke means more force per push. I went looking for evidence that a particular cadence protects the knee and it is mixed, so I did not build the cue on it. The one paper I fetched supporting it (Ebbecke, Hansen, Nackel, Viellehner & Potthast, ISB Stockholm 2025 conference abstract, https://fis.dshs-koeln.de/en/publications/knee-joint-loading-during-cycling-should-osteoarthritis-patients-/) tested 12 male ACTIVE cyclists with diagnosed knee osteoarthritis, age 57.3 +/- 7.9, BMI 25.7 +/- 2.9, at 157 to 261 W, and states verbatim "The only exceptions were KAMpeak at 157 W and 210 W between 60 and 80 rpm", so at the low power outputs a beginner actually rides, 60 to 80 rpm made no significant difference to peak knee load. Wrong age, wrong BMI, joint disease he does not have, powers above what he will hold, and not peer reviewed.

cues.name: Do not touch the resistance before 2:00
cues.cue: Set the resistance in the first 15 seconds of each 4 minute effort and then leave it completely alone until 2:00. At 30 and 60 seconds the watch will look too low. That is normal: on a bike the heart rate takes over a minute to arrive. Cranking the resistance at 40 seconds because the watch says 128 is the single most likely way a first interval session goes wrong. At 2:00 you make one decision, in a fixed order, cadence first and then heart rate, and then you ride out the last two minutes. Also expect the resistance level to be LOWER in the last interval than in the first.
cues.test: At 2:00 into each 4 minute effort, one look, two readouts, at most one change. (1) RPM below 70? Drop one resistance level and stop there, no heart rate check this interval. (2) Otherwise, heart rate 150 to 165: change nothing. Under 150: add one level. Over 165: drop one level. No further changes until the next effort, with two standing overrides that beat this rule at any second: if you have to come off the seat to turn the pedals, drop a level, and if a stop rule fires, stop. The session succeeded if every effort ended with heart rate between 150 and 165. Whether the resistance number went up, down, or nowhere is not part of that test.
cues.why: The load-bearing fact, that heart rate lags well over a minute on a bike, is sourced twice and is the whole reason the 2:00 checkpoint exists. The single-decision design and the falling-number reassurance are my convention layered on top of that fact, not findings, and the falling number is deliberately not a success criterion because a session where all four efforts landed in the band is a good session whatever the resistance did.
cues.grounding: Two papers, both fetched. (1) Tjonna et al., EX-MET protocol, BMC Public Health 2018, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5879994/: the 4x4 arm specifies the interval target heart rate is "reached within two minutes". (2) Acala JJ, Roche-Willis D, Astorino TA. "Characterizing the Heart Rate Response to the 4 x 4 Interval Exercise Protocol." Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2020;17(14):5103. 39 healthy ACTIVE adults (20 M, 19 F, age 26.0 +/- 6.1, body mass 72.1 +/- 10.8 kg, BMI 24.2 +/- 2.9, VO2max 37.0 +/- 5.4) on a Velotron cycle ergometer: roughly 1.3 min to reach 85% HRmax in interval 1; time in the 85-95% band 2.7 +/- 0.6 min in interval 1 versus 3.4 to 3.5 min in intervals 2 to 4; 12.9 +/- 0.4 of 16 min overall; mean power 75%, 63%, 59% and 54% of peak power output across intervals 1 to 4. Three things that paper does NOT support and that I am therefore not claiming: its authors did not recommend setting resistance once, their method "continually adjusted [power] in steps of +/-5% PPO" off real-time heart rate and raised the work rate "at any point... that HR declined by >= 2 b/min"; the falling power was produced by that investigator control, not observed in self-paced riders; and the paper states its "data cannot be applied to older, inactive, or highly trained populations", which puts him outside it.

cues.name: Stay on the seat
cues.cue: Stay seated for every effort. Standing up is not a way to make an interval harder, and on a gym upright with flat pedals and street shoes it is not a skill you have yet. If the only way you can turn the pedals is to lift off the seat, the resistance is one level too high, full stop.
cues.test: Any moment during a 4 minute effort when your backside leaves the seat: sit back down and drop one resistance level immediately. No judgement about how briefly, and this override beats the 2:00 rule.
cues.why: All that paper supports is the narrow claim that standing does not change the metabolic cost of the work, in elite cyclists on a real bike. That standing is a bad idea for a heavy rider on a gym upright is my judgement, not a finding: it costs him cadence control and it is the usual way "too much resistance" turns into a knee problem instead of into a dropped level.
cues.grounding: Carlsson M, Lindblom O, Carlsson T. Front Sports Act Living. 2024;6:1395415. Ten elite male cyclists (age 25 +/- 8, mass 75.9 +/- 8.4 kg), 5 min bouts at 6.8 degrees incline. Seated versus standing showed no significant difference in oxygen uptake (3.86 +/- 0.45 vs 3.86 +/- 0.42 L/min) or gross efficiency (21.3 +/- 1.2 vs 21.3 +/- 1.1 percent), identical to three significant figures. The study's actual primary comparison was a third condition, repeated seated/standing transitions (3.94 +/- 0.45 L/min, 21.0 +/- 1.1 percent), which is not what this cue is about.

cues.name: What stops the effort
cues.cue: KNEE: any sharp pain in or around the knee, or any ache that gets worse across an effort rather than staying level. Stop the effort, spin easy at the recovery resistance to the end of the session, and do not do the remaining efforts. CHEST: pressure or pain in the chest, or pain spreading into the jaw, neck or left arm. Stop, get off, tell staff, and talk to a doctor before you finish or drive anywhere. HEAD: dizziness, feeling faint, going cold and clammy, or your vision going patchy at the edges. Stop, get off, and sit down on the floor rather than on a machine. HEART RATE ABOVE {PEAK_BPM}, the top of your recorded range: drop to the recovery resistance for two minutes, check the watch strap is snug first because a loose wrist sensor reads high, then decide whether the session continues. Everything else on this page is "drop one level and carry on". These are not.
cues.test: Before each effort starts, one sentence to yourself: "chest, head, knee". Anything other than normal in any of the three, and the effort does not start. During an effort, if anything above is present AT ALL, you stop rather than adjust. There is no severity judgement to make, presence is the whole test.
cues.why: I looked for a citable plain-language stop list for unsupervised interval training and did not find one I could read. What exists is ACSM's criteria for terminating a supervised exercise TEST, with a technician and an ECG in the room, and dressing that up as a source for a man alone on a gym bike would be exactly the kind of fake grounding this exercise is meant to catch. It is here because the alternative was no stop rule at all.

bike.cuesNote:
WHAT WAS DROPPED FROM THIS SET, one line each. The full reasoning is in the file, not on this page.

1. THE SADDLE FORE-AND-AFT RULE. No peer-reviewed support, and the test was broken two ways: both branches described the same geometry while prescribing opposite fixes. Leave the seat in the middle and write the notch number down next to the height.
2. HANDLEBAR HEIGHT. No evidence isolating it, no test he can perform while sitting on the saddle, and many gym uprights have fixed bars so the prescribed fix may not exist.
3. "INTERVAL 4 SHOULD BE ONE TO THREE LEVELS BELOW INTERVAL 1." The source reports percentages of peak power; a gym resistance level is an arbitrary manufacturer scale with no fixed watt value.
4. A CLAIM ABOUT WHAT ACALA'S AUTHORS RECOMMEND. I fetched the paper and they did close to the opposite of what the note said.
5. RE-READING YOUR MAXIMUM HEART RATE OFF INTERVAL 4 AND REVISING THE BAND UP. That turns interval 4 into a maximal test, which is a different and higher-risk session than the one you agreed to.
6. "HIGHER CADENCE REDUCED KNEE LOAD AT EVERY POWER LEVEL." The source says the opposite at the power levels that apply to you.
7. THREE CONTRADICTORY RULES FOR THE 1:00 MARK. There is now one checkpoint at 2:00, cadence first then heart rate.

MYTHS I AM CONFIDENT ENOUGH TO NAME

- "Get the saddle height slightly wrong and you will wreck your knees." Not supported. Bini & Priego-Quesada 2022, 41 studies: limited evidence on saddle-height changes and injury risk, and moderate evidence that changes under 4 percent of leg length produce trivial to small changes in lower-limb loads and no effect on oxygen uptake or efficiency. For a 90 cm leg that is roughly 3.5 cm of tolerance. Reproducing the same setting is worth more than measuring an angle, which is why the cue asks him to write a number down rather than hit 25 degrees.
- "Standing up makes the interval harder." It does not make the work cost more. Seated and standing were identical to three significant figures for oxygen uptake and gross efficiency in the study I read. It moves where the force comes from, that is all.
- "Your heart rate should be in the zone in the first minute." No. Measured lag was about 1.3 minutes in interval 1, and even with an investigator adjusting power every 15 seconds, only 2.7 of that interval's 4 minutes were spent in the band. Interval 1 is always the worst one for time in zone, by design of physiology and not by his failure.

$cuesArchive.dropped:
WHAT I DROPPED, AND WHY

1. SADDLE FORE AND AFT (the KOPS rule). Dropped entirely. It had no peer-reviewed support to begin with, and the test was broken in two ways at once: both branches described the identical geometry (spindle ahead of kneecap = kneecap behind spindle) while prescribing opposite corrections, and one of them was inverted. It also depends on where his head is rather than where his knee is, so leaning forward two inches flips the answer with the saddle untouched. It contradicted the saddle-height cue's own premise as well: if strangers move the seat post they move the seat rail. If his bike's seat slides, the honest one-liner is "leave it in the middle, write the notch number next to the height, put it back there each visit". That does not need a cue.

2. HANDLEBAR HEIGHT. Dropped. Three failures and no evidence: the Cureus bike-fit review isolates nothing about bar height, "set the bars level with the saddle" has no test he can perform while sitting on the saddle, and many gym uprights have fixed bars, so the prescribed fix ("raise them one notch") may not exist. The only part worth keeping is a sentence, not a cue: if you are propping your upper body up on your arms you are unloading the seat and quietly undoing the height you just set.

3. "INTERVAL 4 SHOULD BE ONE TO THREE LEVELS BELOW INTERVAL 1" AS A SUCCESS CRITERION. Dropped outright, and it was the worst item in the draft. Acala reports 75, 63, 59 and 54 percent of PEAK POWER OUTPUT. Gym resistance levels are an arbitrary manufacturer scale with no fixed watt value, so a 28 percent relative power drop cannot be converted into "one to three levels" from that paper or any other. Worse, as a pass/fail it manufactures a false failure: he could finish all four efforts in the heart rate band and be told the session did not succeed. The falling number survives only as reassurance inside the 2:00 cue, never as a target, and the success test is now heart rate alone.

4. THE CLAIM THAT ACALA'S AUTHORS "RECOMMEND PRESCRIBING BY POWER OUTPUT RATHER THAN CHASING HEART RATE MID-INTERVAL". Deleted. I fetched the paper and they did close to the opposite: power was "continually adjusted in steps of +/-5% PPO" to hold 85-95% HRmax, and "at any point during any interval that HR declined by >= 2 b/min, work rate was increased by 5% PPO". The 2:00 rule is now grounded on the measured lag (about 1.3 min to 85% HRmax) plus EX-MET's own "reached within two minutes", and the why says plainly that the single-decision design is my convention on top of a sourced fact.

5. THE PROPOSAL TO RE-READ HIS MAXIMUM HEART RATE OFF INTERVAL 4 IN WEEKS 3 AND 4 AND REVISE THE BAND UPWARD. Dropped. That turns interval 4 into a maximal test in an untrained beginner at his current bodyweight (read HealthOS/CURRENT.md; a figure typed here goes stale silently and one was, 104.9 against a live 103.7), which is a different and higher-risk activity than the 4x4 he agreed to, and it ratchets every absolute target upward with no ceiling. His plan says 150 to 165. A cue sheet is not the place to renegotiate that upward. The honest caveat survives in cue 3 and its FACT was corrected on 2026-08-28: 175 is not the highest figure his watch has recorded. The export's highest is {PEAK_BPM} and 23 of 60 swims beat 175, so the bands are low by a wider margin than this note believed. The direction of the caveat is unchanged and the bands are unchanged.

6. "HIGHER CADENCE REDUCED KNEE LOAD AT EVERY POWER LEVEL". Deleted, because the source says the opposite in one place and it is the place that matters. Verified verbatim at the fetched URL: "The only exceptions were KAMpeak at 157 W and 210 W between 60 and 80 rpm". At the low power outputs a beginner rides, going from 60 to 80 rpm did NOT significantly reduce peak knee adduction moment, and that is precisely the comparison the prescription rested on. The whole knee-load argument is now a disclosed caveat and the cadence cue is labelled CONVENTION, justified by bookkeeping and by arithmetic (power = force x pedal speed) rather than by a study.

7. THREE CONTRADICTORY RULES FOR THE 1:00 MARK. The draft had cadence saying "check at 1:00, 2:00 and 3:00 and drop a level if RPM is below 75", the interval cue saying "no other checks during the four minutes", and a third cue adding a check at 1:00 of intervals 2 to 4. Worse, the cadence rule "RPM above 90 and heart rate under 150, add a level" fires almost automatically at 1:00 in interval 1, because the same document's own source says heart rate takes 1.3 minutes to arrive. There is now ONE checkpoint, 2:00, with a fixed priority order (cadence first, then heart rate) and exactly two standing overrides (off the seat, stop rule). The 85-to-90 RPM dead zone between the cue and its own test is gone.
$cuesArchive.couldNotGround:
WHAT I SEARCHED FOR AND COULD NOT GROUND

- Helgerud 2007, the original Norwegian 4x4. Not fetched, not cited anywhere. Everything asserted about the protocol comes from EX-MET and Acala, both of which I opened.
- A training RCT of the 4x4 on a bike in untrained or obese adults. I could not find one. What exists is the identical protocol on the identical machine in a clinical population (EX-MET, metabolic syndrome) and an acute heart-rate characterisation on a cycle ergometer in healthy ACTIVE young adults (Acala, mean BMI 24.2, mean age 26). The prescription for a 34-year-old BMI 33 beginner is a defensible extrapolation, not a tested one, and Acala says in its own limitations that its data "cannot be applied to older, inactive... populations".
- Peveler 2008 on saddle height and economy, the primary behind the widely repeated 25-35 degree figure. CORRECTED 2026-09-03: this entry said it was "paywalled at every mirror. Not cited" and that neither paper "tested it". The FULL TEXT is paywalled; the ABSTRACT is free on PubMed and is now saved at HealthOS/knowledge/sources/peveler-2008-saddle-height-economy.txt. It reports a real test: 15 subjects, 5 cyclists and 10 non-cyclists, 15 minutes at the resistance giving 70% of VO2max, comparing a 25 degree knee angle against a 35 degree angle and against 109% of inseam. VO2 was significantly LOWER at 25 degrees than at either of the other two, with no difference in heart rate or perceived exertion, and it concludes in favour of 25 degrees. So 25-35 is indeed quoted as background in that paper, and within the band 25 was tested and won on economy. A degree number is therefore available and defensible, on 15 people at one intensity, and putting one in the cue is a change nobody has made yet.
- Anything peer-reviewed isolating fore/aft saddle position or handlebar height. Nothing. Both cues dropped rather than dressed up with a bike-fitting blog.
- A citable stop-symptom list for unsupervised training. Not found. The ACSM material I located is for supervised, monitored exercise testing, which is a different setting, so the stop cue is labelled CONVENTION and says why.
- Cadence and knee load in anyone resembling him. Genuinely mixed: search surfaced findings in both directions (a 29 percent lower patellofemoral force at 90 vs 70 rpm in one study, no cadence effect on joint forces in another). I did not fetch those, so I have not cited them, and I did not build the cue on knee load.

WHAT THE PLAN ITSELF STILL GETS WRONG

1. "10 min easy" and "3 min easy" carry no numbers, which is exactly the feeling-based instruction the house style bans. Cue 3 supplies 105-123 and 88-123, and note they are two different bands, not one.
2. Nothing tells him to record and restore the seat height on a machine strangers reset weekly. Cue 1 does.
3. No stop condition anywhere on the bike, although the run half has one. Cue 7 does.
4. 43 minutes is his structure, not the published one. EX-MET's session is 38 minutes because there is no recovery after interval 4. Harmless, but the 43 should not be presented as coming from the protocol.
5. HRpeak in the protocol means a peak from a maximal test. Neither 175 nor {PEAK_BPM} is that. And 175 was not even his highest recorded reading, which is a separate and worse error corrected 2026-08-28: it was the most common ceiling in his swim data, six sessions tie there, and {PEAK_BPM} sits above it. Every heart-rate figure on this route is interpolated from the database now rather than typed, so this class cannot recur. Flagged in the cue he will actually read, not just here.

OUT OF SCOPE: I did not check Wilson 2012, the interference-effect study behind putting the hard aerobic work on the bike instead of the treadmill. That rationale is his and unverified by me.

$comment: THE REST RULE. Decided by Silvio on 2026-08-21 after a session that laid the load out in front
of him: four days completely off (2026-08-10 to 08-13), then seven consecutive training days
(08-14 to 08-20), gym every one of them, a swim on six, plus a 06:10 treadmill run and a 06:10
bike. He was asked how many days off and whether it should be a fixed day or a rule. He chose
the rule: never more than three in a row.
The audit finding this answers is that the problem was never chronic overload, it was the SWING.
A fixed rest day would not have caught that run, because a seven-day block straddles any
weekday you nominate. A weekly minute cap would not have caught it either: those seven days
were mostly normal-length sessions, and the thing that was unusual was their density.
WHAT MAKES THIS A RULE AND NOT DECORATION. Two mechanisms, per HOODII/.agents/ENGINEERING.md:
1. content/gym/validate.mjs recomputes the PLANNED week from program.json plus assignedDays
below and exits non-zero if the plan itself breaks maxConsecutive. A programme that
contradicts its own rest rule cannot be deployed.
2. /gym/conditioning counts ACTUAL consecutive days from health_watch_session, which is the
watch and not the app, and prints the count against the rule. It reports what happened; it
does not congratulate him.
AND WHAT IT DOES NOT KNOW. Sleep and HRV are the only measurements that could turn this rule from
arithmetic on load into a recovery observation, and they are too sparse to do it: the 2026-08-26
export holds two nights of sleep between 2026-08-15 and the 26th. The rows themselves are there,
24,864 sleep stages and 1,451 HRV readings running to 2026-08-23, so the problem is coverage and
not a dead feed. The watch is worn all day and taken off at night. So this rule is arithmetic on
load, not a recovery measurement, and the page says so
whenever health_recovery is stale.
THE LAST LINE HERE USED TO READ 'wearing the watch to bed is the cheapest thing in this project
and it is what would turn the rule into an observation'. IT IS DELETED, on his answer of
2026-09-03: 'sleeping will always be eincosjsten beacuse I dont wear the watch to sleep'. That is
settled, so do not propose it again, do not price it as a cheap win, and do not open a question
about it. A suggestion left standing in a file gets re-proposed by whoever reads the file next,
which is the whole reason this paragraph replaces it rather than simply removing the sentence.
AND THE SPARSE ROWS ARE NOT A SAMPLE OF HIS NIGHTS. He wears it to sleep rarely, so a night
reaches these tables only when something unusual kept it on, which is why every parse returned
short late nights. See restRule.$caveatChanged for the full reasoning. No sleep or recovery
figure goes on a page, and that is permanent rather than pending a better parse.

restRule.rule: Never more than 3 training days in a row.
whyThisShape: You asked for a rule rather than a fixed day off, and the data says that was right.
The 2026-08-14 to 08-20 block was seven days of ordinary sessions. Nothing in it was too long or
too heavy. What was unusual was that none of them had a gap, and it followed four days of
nothing. A fixed Sunday off does not catch a block that runs Friday to Thursday. A weekly minute
ceiling does not catch it either, because the minutes were normal. Density was the thing, so
density is what the rule counts.
whatCountsAsTraining: Any session the watch recorded that is not walking: lifting, swimming, treadmill, bike, and
A day with only a walk on it is a rest day, however long the walk was. You walked 80 minutes and
5.7 km on 2026-08-16 and that day still counts as rest.
Counted from the WATCH, not from the gym app. The app only sees sessions you opened it for, and
that is a smaller number, so counting the app would report rest you did not take.
restRule.whenItFires: On the fourth consecutive day. It does not block anything: it tells you how many days are behind you and that the next one should be off.
restRule.theHonestCaveat: Three is your number, not a finding. No study sets it, and no measurement of your own recovery supports it: you do not wear the watch to sleep, so there is no recovery series to read and there is not going to be one. It is a sensible ceiling on density, chosen by the person doing the training.
restRule.$caveatChanged:
CORRECTED 2026-09-03, and the correction is smaller than it looks: the conclusion was right and the reason had gone stale.

It read "because sleep and HRV stopped on 2026-08-15". THAT WAS TRUE WHEN WRITTEN on 2026-08-21, six dark nights into a gap. It is not true now, and it was being rendered as a present-tense fact. Counted on 2026-09-03 from the 2026-08-26 export: com.samsung.health.sleep_stage holds 24,864 rows running to 2026-08-23, and com.samsung.health.hrv holds 1,451 rows running to the same day. Neither stopped.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE IS WORSE THAN A STOP AND BETTER THAN A STOP. The rows exist, but from 2026-08-15 to the export on the 26th there are TWO distinct sleep dates, the 15th and the 23rd, and three HRV dates, the 15th, 22nd and 23rd. So the series is too sparse to read a recovery trend from, which is exactly the conclusion the caveat draws. The rule stands. Only the sentence explaining it was wrong, and the wrong version was the flattering-to-nobody kind: it said the measurement was impossible when the measurement is merely absent, which is a thing he can change by wearing the watch.

NO SLEEP DURATION IS QUOTED HERE, DELIBERATELY, AND NONE SHOULD BE ADDED UNTIL THE PARSE IS VALIDATED. The previous session parsed these tables four ways and every combination returned medians between 3.7 and 5.3 hours with bedtimes between 3 and 8 am, which contradicts his own account of his nights. When a parse disagrees with the person who slept, the parse is the suspect. Everything above is a ROW COUNT and a DATE RANGE, which are safe to state because they do not depend on interpreting stage codes or time offsets. The next step is one night he can confirm from memory, checked against what the tables say for that night, before any figure goes anywhere near a page.

HE ANSWERED THAT ON 2026-09-03 AND IT CLOSES THE WHOLE LINE OF ENQUIRY: "sleeping will always be eincosjsten beacuse I dont wear the watch to sleep". DO NOT ASK AGAIN, and do not queue the one-night validation above: it was written expecting a data problem and this is not one.

THE PARSE WAS PROBABLY NEVER WRONG, and that is the part worth carrying. Four parses returning medians of 3.7 to 5.3 hours with bedtimes between 3 and 8 am were treated as evidence against the PARSE, on the reasoning that when a parse disagrees with the person who slept the parse is the suspect. That reasoning assumed the rows were a sample of his nights. They are not. He wears the watch to sleep rarely, so a night only appears here when something unusual kept it on his wrist, and the recorded nights are short and late BECAUSE those are the nights it survived. The numbers were describing the sample honestly; the label "his sleep" was the false part.

SO NO SLEEP OR RECOVERY FIGURE GOES ON ANY PAGE, and this is not "until the parse is validated" any more. The sample is biased by the thing that creates it, so more rows make it more precise and no less wrong. A sleep chart built from this would get sharper and stay false. The only honest uses are a row count and a date range, which is what the caveat above now states.

AND THE RULE IS UNAFFECTED, which is worth saying plainly because the caveat sits under it. The three-day ceiling was never derived from sleep data; it is his call about his own density, and it was his call before any of this was measured.

howItFits.title: Why four things and not one
howItFits.lead: Lifting, swimming, running and the bike are not four hobbies competing for the week. Three of them are free and one has a price, and the plan is built around which is which.

points.claim: Swimming and cycling cost your lifts nothing.
points.detail: A meta-analysis that separated the endurance MODALITY found running, but not cycling, produced significant losses in both strength and size. Swimming carries no eccentric loading either. So the aerobic base can grow on those two without paying for it at the rack.

points.claim: Running is the one that costs, so it is kept short rather than rare.
points.detail: In the same analysis, endurance DURATION correlated more strongly with losses than frequency did. Short and frequent beats long and occasional, which is also exactly what the injury evidence for a novice runner at your bodyweight says.
points.source: Wilson 2012, plus Bertelsen 2018 on novice runners

points.claim: Doing all of it beats doing one of them, on both scoreboards.
points.detail: Against lifting alone, adding endurance left strength, power and size statistically unchanged and improved aerobic capacity. Against endurance alone, adding lifting improved strength substantially. There is no version of this where dropping one makes the others better.

points.claim: Lift first when both happen the same day.
points.detail: No significant effect either way, but the trend favours lifting before the aerobic piece. You already stack the swim after the gym, so this one is a description of what you do rather than a change.

points.claim: And what the rower is for.
points.detail: Non-impact aerobic volume that running would otherwise have to supply, at a price running charges and a machine does not. Two easy fifteen-minute rows before any interval is written: nobody here has rowed, and the first honest hard piece on a new machine is a shock. The bike did this job until 2026-09-04 and comes back if he asks.

howItFits.sourceNote: Full citations and the numbers behind each line are in HealthOS/knowledge/training-programme-evidence.md, section 2.
